items.body: The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other.   Consumers finds its second wind Manic by Drift   Alive & Thriving by Radius Etc   There’s a good story behind why this review exists at all. The Consumers Research and Development Label ran independently through the 2000s before becoming an imprint of Someoddpilot Records, the Chicago label-turned-agency that also handled branding for Pitchfork back when that meant something specific in the industry, and later built brand identity work for clients like Drag City, Jagjaguwar, and Secretly Canadian. Geoffrey Wilson bought Consumers in 2023 with help from Chris Eichenseer, who founded Someoddpilot in 1999 and who Wilson had shared an office with from 2003 to 2008, before the label originally shut down. Somewhere in the years between closing and reopening, a flood destroyed the entire back stock. Whatever’s floating around on Discogs or eBay now is all that survived physically; the rest is gone. The label came back properly in November 2024 with a showcase at Public Works in Wicker Park, quiet after that, and this is its real reintroduction to a wider audience: two EPs, two very different sounds, one label figuring out what it wants to be the second time around. Drift’s Manic comes first and it’s a strange kind of debut for someone who’s clearly not new to any of this. Sean Krainik has run Parotic Records, the Midwest techno label, for over two decades, putting out records from DJ Slip, Johannes Heil, Matt Paffel, Dave Olson, and Mr. Projectile among others. He never released his own music on vinyl until now. Manic pulls from more than twenty years of writing tracks in the background while other people’s records took priority, and that accumulated time shows in how confidently unshowy this record is. This leans techno and IDM more than anything experimental, dancefloor-facing and beat-heavy across the whole tracklist. The title track builds itself up layer by layer into a pulsating beat while TV dialogue keeps pulling focus sideways, a small disruption that never fully resolves. Nothing here is trying to be difficult, and nothing here needed to be. “R$W” and “Osmosis” are the two that stick hardest. Different rhythms, same underlying intent—Krainik chasing something gritty and repetitive at once, loops that don’t evolve so much as they insist on themselves. Baby Ford‘s influence is audible in how minimal and slightly off-center the drum programming stays, that same stripped tension where less becomes the entire point rather than a limitation working against the track. “Murderer’s Row” leans into that same lineage even more directly, carrying an unintended tribute to Throbbing Gristle in its haze and darkness, deliberately murky where the rest of the EP stays brighter. It’s dance music built by someone who spent twenty years listening to other people make dance music, which sounds like it should produce something derivative and instead produces something oddly assured. He knows exactly which two or three elements a track actually needs and refuses to add a fourth just because he can.   Two EPs, two very different sounds :: Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving sits nowhere near that world. This is instrumental hip-hop pushed somewhere stranger, call it hip-hop IDM for lack of a cleaner label, though the term undersells how much dub techno and straight experimental electronic music bleeds into the beats underneath. Norwood recorded this across a blur of hostels, planes, and temporary housing between 2021 and 2025, and the press notes frame it explicitly as documentation of moving from housing instability and food scarcity into something closer to self-actualization. A travel document, in his own words, proof of surviving into thriving. That context sits underneath the music without ever being spelled out inside the tracks themselves, which is the right call. The record doesn’t lecture you about where it came from. It just carries the weight of it. “Goldenlocks” is the standout, and it’s also the most straightforwardly hip-hop beat on the record, except the tempo keeps breaking and the snares reverse and catch themselves mid-hit like the whole beat is tripping over its own feet on purpose. There’s a video for it, one of three the label produced for this release. Little vocal samples surface throughout, adding texture without ever becoming a hook. “Stuttering Spaces (PoplockJam)” goes fully electro, upbeat in a way nothing else on the record quite matches, the most purely fun three minutes here. “One 4 Larry Heard Pt. 1” is the only track running a straight 4/4 kick and it’s catchy specifically because it doesn’t try to be clever about it, same DNA as everything surrounding it just aimed squarely at a dancefloor instead of a headspace. The “Pt. 1” leaves you wondering if there’s a Pt. 2 coming or if the numbering is its own quiet joke about unfinished business. “Go Inside/Outside” is the most abstract piece on the record, a loop cycling endlessly through filters and phasers and pitch shifts like a revolving door that never fully closes, always mid-swing. The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other. They just happen to share a home. If these two EPs are the tone-setters for what Consumers wants to be in its second life, the label picked back up somewhere considerably more interesting than where it left off two decades ago. Drift‘s Manic and Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving are both available on The Consumers Research and Development Label. items.body: Analogical Force has long occupied the productive tension between experimentation and the dancefloor’s accumulated memory. Hidden Soul sits firmly within that tension, fluent in its established language and meticulously composed. But perhaps the most exciting possibility lies just beyond that fluency: not abandoning the listener, but trusting them enough to take the familiar somewhere unfamiliar. Muscle memory and accumulated emotional shorthand [AF069] Hidden Soul EP by The 89th Passenger   The 89th Passenger returns to the release schedule of one of contemporary dance music’s more compelling production houses with Hidden Soul, from Paris-based Jeremy Cohen delivering five tidy, DJ-friendly excursions into the familiar architecture of breaks, pads, subs and euphorically melancholic atmospheres. This is music that understands the dancefloor not as a problem requiring reinvention, but as an existing language, complete with its own grammar, muscle memory and accumulated emotional shorthand. “Paper Wings” establishes that grammar almost immediately. Chopped breaks, rounded subs, 303 squiggles and luminous pads are looped into clean, recognisable frames, each element occupying its expected orbit. There is something almost architectural about the neatness of it: familiar components assembled into a functioning environment designed to communicate quickly, cleanly and without obstruction. “Hidden Soul” pushes further into the low end, drawing on break patterns whose familiarity is part of their appeal. Its immediacy is hard to resist; the rhythmic language seems already lodged somewhere in the listener’s body. “What it Takes to Fly” lightens the palette considerably, pairing pretty 303 work with gorgeous tones and gently arpeggiating synths. Its carefully managed peaks, troughs and breakdowns possess an almost cinematic emotional shorthand—the kind of musical optimism that could soundtrack an airplane disappearing into a sunrise. Music interested in making the familiar feel good :: “Eren” continues along those coordinates, allowing textures to breathe while the rhythmic components settle into a quiet, efficient momentum. It feels less like a departure than another room in the same building: different light, familiar construction. “Analog Serenade” finally shifts the pace and texture again, suggesting another route through the material without substantially redrawing its map. And this is where the record becomes more interesting as an artefact of contemporary dance music. Its boundaries are visible. This is not music attempting to make the familiar unstable; it is music interested in making the familiar feel good. The breaks remain breaks, the 303 remains gloriously 303, and the emotional trajectory arrives largely where expectation has already placed it. There is safety here, but it is designed safety: a deliberate perimeter around the possibility of surprise. Yet accessibility and predictability are not the same thing. Music can push its own materials beyond their comfort zone without alienating the listener. In fact, some of the most generous dance music does precisely this, inviting you into a recognisable room before quietly moving the walls. Safety can be useful, but it can also become lazy—an easy creative cheat in which recognition performs the emotional labour that invention might otherwise have to do. Analogical Force has long occupied the productive tension between experimentation and the dancefloor’s accumulated memory. Hidden Soul sits firmly within that tension, fluent in its established language and meticulously composed. But perhaps the most exciting possibility lies just beyond that fluency: not abandoning the listener, but trusting them enough to take the familiar somewhere unfamiliar. items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. items.body: Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. An accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation landscape 07 by fields we found / quiet details   Fields We Found is the alias of British musician, mastering engineer and visual artist Alex Gold, who founded the quiet details label in 2023. Following releases on Home Normal, Seil Records, handstitched*, and Ambientologist, Gold has increasingly focused his work on extended listening. The Landscape series grew out of compositions created for his personal meditation practice; over time, the creative process itself also became a form of meditation. Landscape 07, the seventh installment in the series, runs for more than twenty-five minutes. It is an extended live performance constructed from electronic instruments, tape and successive layers of sound. The piece begins almost without a threshold. A broad sound emerges from the haze, already inhabited by tremors, gentle fluctuations and distant trails. During the opening minutes, the music gains weight; the volume rises calmly and glimmers of light move across its surface. From here, Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. “Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined.” ~Mirco Salvadori The presence of tape can be felt in the sound’s internal movement. The notes have porous edges, slight instabilities and a warmth far removed from artificial stillness. Even when everything appears motionless, something continues to shift. The overall balance gradually changes, brighter colours surface and the mass of sound seems to lift. Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined. Gold handles duration with patience and restraint. Each event is allowed to remain long enough to alter our perception of everything around it. In its central section, the piece takes on a darker, more introspective colour. Threads and reflections continue to move through the texture; through headphones, they reveal small lateral movements, like currents. Light then returns gradually and the music expands without losing its composure. This leads to the point of greatest emotional intensity, reached through patient accumulation. The journey feels natural, almost as though it had formed by itself, while retaining the freedom of a gesture made in the moment. The piece asks for a simple kind of openness: to remain, to listen, to give each nuance time to reveal itself and to accept that the inner landscape may change alongside the sonic one. In these passages, distant echoes of German electronic music from the early 1970s begin to surface. The more abstract expanses of Tangerine Dream’s Zeit, the cosmic materiality of early Klaus Schulze and some of Cluster’s suspended atmospheres come to mind in the way timbre becomes form. Fields We Found keeps everything on an intimate, tactile scale. The connection lies in the trust placed in machines, in their natural drift and in the time a sound needs to reveal its hidden folds. Recording the performance directly to tape preserves the element of risk that gives life to such a gradual process. “A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception.” ~Mirco Salvadori An even closer affinity leads to Éliane Radigue. Landscape 07 shares the French composer’s attentiveness to what can emerge from within a prolonged sound and to the variations that appear when the ear stops searching for a melody. The historical and poetic distance remains clear; the surface here is denser and more explicitly ambient. Yet the kind of listening it requires is close to Radigue’s: focused, patient and ready to recognise an event within apparent stillness. Pauline Oliveros’ Deep Listening also comes to mind, particularly in its understanding of attention as an active part of the work, as does Suzanne Ciani, in the gentle way electronic sound can suggest physical movement. Towards the end, the piece begins to subtract. The pressure recedes, its lines grow sparse and what remains reveals its irregularities more clearly. The farewell becomes fragile. The long fade avoids any emphatic sense of closure. A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception. It is an ending fully consistent with the work as a whole: the ear is left to measure the disappearance, while the silence that follows seems to last a little longer. Landscape 07 succeeds because its calmness contains tension. Meditation here has density, pressure and material memory. The instruments breathe, the tapes impart instability and depth, and the studio work preserves the spontaneity of the performance. With each new listen, the hierarchy of details changes: something that first seemed marginal becomes a guide, a fluctuation turns into rhythm, a blur acquires definition. This is music that entrusts its richness to time and draws its strength from time in return. A remarkable entry in the series, and perhaps its most accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation. Landscape 07 is available on quiet details. items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — Echorec featured in Prog magazine 106 (February 2020) in an article titled 16 bands to watch this year, before their debut album The Island had even been released. Currently based in Bath, the trio easily deserve a place in that list because The Island is an incredibly mature offering. They even had the audacity to attempt, and successfully pull off a subtle interpretation of the end section of Pink Floyd's Echoes during the 17 minute long closing track The Lamb Returns ? Pink Floyd, listed as 'an artist we also like', being one of the leading exponents of the Binson Echorec analogue delay effect which provided the young band with their name. Made up of Julian Kirk (vocals, guitars and keyboards), Brad McGinty (bass, vocals) and Jake Aubrey (drums and percussion), there's no compromise in the quality or quantity of either lead instrument; Kirk is a genuine multi-instrumentalist who can play stately Gilmour-like guitar but also does an admirable impersonation of Tony Banks playing a fluid ARP solo on The Cinema Show. Despite being momentarily reminded of David Surkamp on Safe at Home (the epigrammatic opener The Water is a piano instrumental) I declined to look for comparisons with Kirk's vocal style because his voice simply seems to fit well with the music. McGinty and Aubrey are also both very capable musicians, meting out inventive rhythm patterns during staccato riffing or bubbling and bouncing along in the melodic sections - this is the essence of the music, it's primarily melodic, it's not derivative, it has plenty of changes and uses a broad palette to produce a nicely-balanced modern prog sound with classic touches.The Island is a concept album that relates the story of a teenage girl's journey of self-discovery. Raised on a lighthouse rock by a single mother who is reluctant to grant her any freedom, she flees to the Island in search of her father. The truth is finally revealed in the epic The Lamb Returns, that her nuclear family fell apart following the early death of her older brother. It's hard to believe that the story isn't personal ? it's well constructed with suitable imagery of yearning, hope, doubt and resolution ? and it's certainly a bold move on a debut release.It's not really a big issue because the entire work is thoroughly commendable, but I don't think the lyrics, which work fine as part of individual song structures and as an overarching narrative, fully rise to the challenge of telling such difficult themes.Stuck in the middle of a pandemic, a streaming-only release is not unreasonable, though getting noticed in a vast industry geared towards rewarding established acts and/or instant gratification isn't going to be easy for a new band with a debut album. In my opinion, the interest generated by exposure through Prog magazine should be maximised by investing in a physical product to be ready for the merchandise stand when gigs resume. I'm pretty sure that Echorec's music will be greeted favourably by the prog community.Three and a half stars

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — I was given the opportunity to review Jordan Rudess' WIRED FOR MADNESS before I'd ever listened to a note played by Dream Theater and equally shocking, I always used to skip over articles about the band in magazines and books. One good thing is that I was able to approach this review, for the keyboard player's fifteenth solo outing, without any idea of what the music would be like, although it's obvious that I've harboured preconceptions about the band he's most associated with. Another thing on the plus side, I know that Rudess is admired by musician friends whose opinions I respect, one of which lent Rudess his Kurzweil K2600 keyboard for a couple of performances organised by the Italian Dreamers during a Rudess family holiday in Italy around the time of Feeding the Wheel. The K2600 still bears Rudess' autograph. The album cover design neatly encapsulates the story behind the title track, an individual who accedes to becoming partially computerised and as his human self is reduced, he undergoes a procedure to upgrade his mental and physical capabilities. As a result he becomes increasingly separated from the outside world with his computerised portion performing the majority of his routine functions, allowing his mind to travel freely between madness and spiritual enlightenment. In a nod to previous prog epics, the track is split into two parts with a total running time of over 34 minutes and maintains a high tempo throughout. Without any Dream Theater reference points I have struggled to draw comparisons but in terms of wild, creative conceptuality and sheer musical density it comes close to Patrick Moraz's Story of i. It could easily have been dreamt up in 1974 and serves as a tribute to the 70's progressive rock keyboard players who influenced Rudess, Rick Wakeman, Keith Emerson and Patrick Moraz included. Having never heard his playing before I had no idea how good Rudess was, with elegant rhapsodic piano, authentic Hammond organ tones, and sinuous synthesizer runs. The modern sounding keyboards remind me of Eddie Jobson's work on the debut UK album and, when the rhythm section gets into a modern-jazz mood, like Dave Stewart on National Health's swansong DS al coda. I'm not a huge fan of the lyrics but they serve the composition well and, delivered by Rudess himself (apart from guest female vocals from Marjana Semkina in the role of an angel, and Dream Theater frontman James LaBrie at the climactic end to part 2), they are well sung. The track is heavy at times but there are sufficient strong melodies and tonal variation, almost all played at a frantic pace, to keep the listener interested. It goes without saying that his guest musicians are all of the highest calibre. With Wired for Madness parts 1 and 2 taking up more than half of the album and close enough to being able to fill a single traditional LP on their own, the remaining tracks run the risk of acting as filler, though this isn't really the case. Off the Ground is a straightforward pleasant, mellow, reflective piece, a welcome respite from the onslaught that's just taken place, but Drop Twist once again picks up the pace following an early arcade game-like intro. It may not be prog as we know it but the short instrumental allows Rudess to show his chops. Perpetual Shrine could almost be Drop Twist part 2, but if anything it's busier and funkier. It wouldn't sound out of place if it was used as the theme music for an 80s TV detective series based somewhere in Florida... The one track that feels to me to be there to make up the numbers is Just Can't Win. I'm being unfair because I'm not a fan of the Blues, but it performs a similar function to ELP's Tiger in a Spotlight, a moment of relief from the technical bombast but still a little self-indulgent. Here Rudess utilises the guitar talents of Joe Bonamassa and incorporates a full brass section; as a blues-rock song it can't be denied that it pushes all the appropriate buttons. Just for Today is another reflective, slow-paced number but it includes sweeping cinematic strokes before it gives way to the jazzy Why I Dream where the vocal phrasing reminds me of Supersister or Jeff Berlin on Gradually Going Tornado. Wired for Madness showcases Rudess' excellent playing and I believe he's pulled off something spectacular with the 34 minute title-track, an excess to rival anything from the 70s. It wasn't nearly as heavy as I'd feared but covers the whole gamut of prog and prog-related styles, with melody, rather than riff taking the lead. Furthermore, the pacy compositions that bookend the recording makes it sound as though the whole writing, playing and recording was fun. Three and a half stars

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Throughout his career, Jon Anderson has not limited himself to the paths of progressive rock. His constant exploration of diverse musical languages - in search of new textures and nuances and free from conventional constraints - has led him to expand his sonic palette and reflect it in musical works of very different natures. "The More You Know" (1998), his twelfth studio album, is one of those works that strays furthest from the genre that made Yes one of its leading standard-bearers.Prioritizing gentle, melodic structures over any display of instrumental virtuosity, "The More You Know" moves, almost effortlessly, through pop and world music sounds, in which the arrangements and programming form the foundation upon which much of the album rests. Songs like "Magic Love," "Say Jocky," and "Take, Take, Take" are easy on the ears but don't seem to offer anything substantial. On the other hand, when the English singer's more spiritual side comes to the fore, some of the album's best moments emerge, including the melancholic "Heaven's Love" and "Sad," and the jubilant "Youth" with its ethnic overtones.Also noteworthy are the arrangements on "Dancing Fool" and the light soul-jazz of "Free (Some Would Say)," underpinned by the deep, expressive bass of Bobby Jocky, brother of Francis Jocky, who contributes on keyboards and as a composer. The rest of the album hovers in an accessible average that never quite takes off, with the standout feature being Anderson's angelic voice, which is in fine form. That's no small thing, but it's not enough to overcome a production that, at times, feels overly polished.2/2.5 stars

The album 'Nine Lives' in particular issubjected to a high-energy, buzzing start, in the face of melodic numbers like 'Insomniac' and'Flowers and Rust', while its ending resorts to mellower, more atmospheric tones that are exploredon the longer songs 'World Without' and 'Prospect for Escape'. Certain instrumental sections are waytoo loud in the recording, especially in the faster tracks in the beginning, but I think thisproblem is taken care of in the second half of the recording. The vocals are fine, but some of thelyrics feel corny, while the album itself strikes you as almost too eclectic, which is probably whatVHB had wanted to do, but this aspect of it may disengage some listeners. I think the main issuewith 'Nine Lives' is the fact that there are very few highlights present. The record is quite solidoverall and the variety of styles covered provides for an engaging listen, but the songs featured onit are mostly hit or miss.

items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Guardians” on October 2, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles dream-pop duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine describe the track as a look back at a period that no longer feels real: “This is a song about looking back on a time in your life that doesn’t feel real anymore, even though it really happened.” “Guardians” is the second track lifted from “Sun Kiss,” a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It follows “Diamond Rain”, issued in mid-August, which was the first single from the same record. Guardians by Magic Wands “Guardians” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. Magic Wands’ 2026 singles and EPs “Guardians” and “Diamond Rain” extend a run of releases that started with “Cascades,” the album Magic Wands issued on October 24, 2025. The duo opened 2026 with “Sacred Mirrors,” a January collaboration with Psychedelic Furs guitarist John Ashton. The six-track “Wishing Well” EP followed in April, and Side-Line reviewed it that August. A six-track “Remixes” EP reworking songs from “Cascades” followed in June. Magic Wands remixed Peter Murphy’s “Swoon” in late spring, and Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville, Tennessee, in the summer of 2008 around vocalists and guitarists Dexy Valentine and Chris Valentine, who began writing together after Dexy moved from Los Angeles to Nashville. The duo later relocated to Los Angeles, where they are now based. Their sound blends dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth textures, carried by layered guitars, droning synths and Dexy’s vocals. The band debuted with the album “Aloha Moon” (Bright Antenna, 2012), preceded by the EP “Magic Love & Dreams” (2009). “Jupiter” followed on Cleopatra Records in 2016, and “Abrakadabra” on Etxe Records & Productions / Casa del Puente Discos in 2018. Magic Wands self-released “Illuminate” in 2020, then signed to Metropolis Records for “Switch,” released May 12, 2023. Side-Line reviewed “Switch” that September, having already covered the duo’s single “Fortune” in April 2022, the single “Time” that May, and the remix album and tour announced that August. Magic Wands’ sixth album, “Cascades,” arrived in October 2025 and set off the run of singles, remixes and EPs that continued through 2026. “Guardians” now carries that chronology into “Sun Kiss,” the duo’s next album, scheduled for early 2027.

items.body: German electro-industrial project Forma Tadre’s 1996 debut album “Navigator” is available on vinyl for the first time, as the opening release on the new label Analog Frontier. This 30th Anniversary Edition is a 2xLP gatefold pressed on 160g Electric Seaglass Blue vinyl, limited to 300 copies, and is sold through Analog Frontier’s Bandcamp page alongside a digital edition. Analog Frontier describes itself as a label dedicated to pressing CD and digital-only albums to vinyl for the first time, and “Navigator” is its debut release. The gatefold carries entirely new artwork built from period polar-expedition photography. The images include work by Herbert G. Ponting, official photographer of the British Antarctic (“Terra Nova”) expedition led by Robert Falcon Scott. The package also includes a double-sided insert with the album’s full lyrics. Side D of the vinyl edition adds two tracks that have never been released before: “First Land,” recorded in 1995, and “No Gene For Fate,” from 1997. Both date from the “Navigator” era of Forma Tadre’s catalogue. The 13-track edition runs: “Navigator (Part One)” “FX on a Human Subject” “Plasmasleep” “Date Unknown” “Navigator (Part Two)” “Serpent Charmer” “Looking Glass Men” “Mesozoic Tree Ferns” “Gates” “Celebrate the Cult” “Navigator (Part Three)” “First Land” “No Gene For Fate” “Navigator” was written, produced and mixed by Andreas Meyer, the sole member of Forma Tadre. Andreas Torkler handled mastering for the original eleven tracks. Meyer mastered “First Land” and “No Gene For Fate” himself, and Steve Eagle did additional mastering for the vinyl cut. B.A. Donahoo designed the new gatefold artwork, with additional art elements by Jared Cote and Steve Eagle. Hansjoerg Schifferer plays guitar on “Serpent Charmer” and “Celebrate the Cult.” The lacquer was cut at Complete Mastering and the vinyl pressed at Onyx Record Press. Originally released in 1996 on the German label Off Beat, “Navigator” was Meyer’s first release as the sole member of Forma Tadre. The album departed stylistically from the project’s earlier three-piece incarnation. “Navigator” centers on a theme of exploration and combines symphonic instrumental passages with EBM tracks. Meyer’s interest in the occult and in H.P. Lovecraft informed tracks including “Date Unknown,” “Celebrate the Cult,” “Gates” and “Mesozoic Tree Ferns.” The 30th Anniversary Edition is available as a digital album and as the limited vinyl edition on Bandcamp. Shipping of physical copies to the EU is currently on hold due to new EU customs policies. Navigator (30th Anniversary Edition) by Forma Tadre About Forma Tadre Forma Tadre began in 1986 as a three-piece band in Lower Saxony, Germany, with Andreas Meyer among its members. Meyer took the project’s name from a portmanteau of Tangerine Dream’s album “Force Majeure,” after Tangerine Dream’s “Phaedra” prompted him to buy his first synthesizer. The band played live and recorded the EP “Brightful Times” in 1987, produced by German producer Robert “Bobby” Giddens, who had also worked with DAF. Two of the three members subsequently left without recording further material. Meyer was the sole member of Forma Tadre by 1994. After the trio dissolved, Haujobb’s Björn Junemann encouraged Meyer to send demo tapes to record labels, which led Off Beat to sign him. In 1996, Meyer released “Navigator” as his first album under the Forma Tadre name, built partly from songs he had written separately from the band under the working title “P-Songs.” Around 1995, Meyer also worked with a female vocalist on a separate, classically-oriented project named Eisriesenkönig, which released a single track on Off Beat’s 1996 compilation “The O-Files.” After “Navigator,” Daniel Myer of Haujobb approached Meyer to collaborate, and the two formed Newt. The duo released two albums and a single between 1997 and 1999. Through the 1990s and 2000s, Meyer produced remixes for acts including Haujobb, La Floa Maldita, New Mind, Wumpscut and Assemblage 23. Forma Tadre’s second album, “Automate,” followed in 1998 and shifted toward a more ambient sound. After close to a decade of silence, Meyer returned Forma Tadre in 2008 with the 13-track album “The Music of Erich Zann,” inspired by H.P. Lovecraft’s short story of the same name. In 2019, “Brightful Times” was reissued as a hybrid vinyl-and-digital edition that added eight tracks recorded between 1987 and 1992 to the original four-track EP. In 2020, Forma Tadre released two archival anthologies. “Navigator Travelogue” collected remixes, singles, demos and unreleased tracks from 1994-1997, and “P-SongX, the hidden path” gathered personal recordings that predated “Navigator.” In 2021, Forma Tadre released “Geiger’s Day”, its first album issued on CD in 20 years. In 2025, the project followed with the digital archival compilation “Seven Century Factory”, which drew on demos and sketches recorded between 1997 and 2007. This reissue follows the 2019 vinyl-and-digital edition of “Brightful Times.” It extends Forma Tadre’s archival reissue campaign to “Navigator,” the project’s 1996 debut album.

items.body: Jesu Aparicio is a Spanish artist who sees himself first and foremost as a DJ, and only secondly as a producer. He has been active in the Spanish club scene for years and won me over this year with his album “Human Control”. The album was released on Jesu’s own label, Espacio Cielo, in collaboration with Mots Music. The name Parissior may not ring a bell for many, but I highly recommend this work to anyone with an interest in Dark-Techno and EBM. The album’s title and theme reflect the increasingly complex relationship between humans, technology, control, and the systems that shape our daily lives. By combining dark electronic sounds with an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intriguing, Parissior creates music that invites the listener to look beyond the surface. The album evokes the atmosphere and danceability of the 1990s Frankfurt Techno scene while adding a distinctly contemporary twist. For me, this record is one of this year’s best discoveries, making it the perfect time to meet the artist behind Parissior and talk to him about “Human Control”, his influences, and his approach to music. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Parissior interview Q: Could you give us some background on your musical activities, which apparently began quite some time ago as a DJ and eventually evolved into producing, leading to the Parissior project? Jesu: I began DJing professionally in my native Cantabria in 2001, playing Techno and House under my own name, ‘Jesu Aparicio’. In 2004, I moved to Salamanca, where I became a resident DJ at several venues, including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz. Those years were a major learning experience for me and gave me a much deeper understanding of the music industry. I eventually opened my own venue, Clavel Ocho, which featured an upstairs floor dedicated to Electronic music called Espacio Cielo – the name I would later revive for my record label. I started producing around 2004 and, over the years, explored many different styles and released music under several aliases. Altogether, I have released more than 600 tracks. I have always considered myself a DJ first and a producer second, although these days I actually spend more time producing music than performing as a DJ. Around 2011, I began to feel restricted by playing the same styles, so I created the Parissior alias as a way to broaden my musical horizons. It allowed me to explore funkier and more cosmic sounds, as well as Electro and Italo-Disco, eventually moving towards the EBM-influenced sound that has become an important part of the project’s identity. Q: Personally, I find it interesting that you moved into music production after starting out as a DJ – a role that naturally exposes you to a vast amount of music. This perhaps also helps explain the eclectic nature of your own work. What did your experience as a DJ bring to your approach to music-making, and what were some of your key influences and muses? Jesu: As a DJ, I have always been very eclectic and curious, and I have always enjoyed collecting music from a wide range of genres: ’80s music, Funk and Soul, Disco, Electro, House, Techno, Big Beat, Breaks… Salamanca had many clubs and bars, each with a very distinct musical identity, so playing there pushed you to dig deeper, discover new sounds and adapt to very different audiences. Being exposed to such a vast amount of music has undoubtedly had a major influence on the way I produce. You learn to recognize the formulas and ideas that make each genre work, and then reinterpret and adapt them to your own musical language. My influences have naturally evolved over the years, but I could never leave out Joy Division and New Order, Talking Heads, The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers, Pet Shop Boys, Andrew Weatherall, Primal Scream or LCD Soundsystem, among many others. Q: You released the album “Human Control” this year, which, as I understand it, was not originally conceived as an album. How did it all come about, and how did the concept of “Human Control” take shape? Or did the concept emerge only afterwards, almost imposing itself on the music? Jesu: As you rightly say, the album was not initially planned as such. I had three tracks that I had deliberately held back from releasing on any label because they felt more personal, less focused on the dancefloor, and did not really fit with any of the EPs I had previously released. Almost without realizing it, I had incorporated phrases and messages into those tracks that shared a certain underlying theme: a defense of the analogue world and a critique of the artificiality and falsehood that often surround today’s digital culture and social media. Once I recognized that common thread, I decided to compose a series of new tracks around those original three and gradually shape the whole thing into an album. The first track I created with that intention was “Human Control.” It features a sample from a speech by Greta Thunberg at the UN Climate Action Summit, in which she delivers a passionate and somewhat dramatic rebuke to the world’s leaders. That track ultimately gave both the album and its central concept a clear identity. Q: What can you tell us about the writing and production process behind the album? What did you focus on most, and what were the different stages you went through to bring “Human Control” to completion? What tools and equipment did you work with, and what were the biggest challenges along the way? Jesu: One of the album’s defining features – and also its biggest challenge – was the decision to deliberately limit the amount of hardware and software I used on each track. I find that working within those kinds of restrictions forces me to be more creative, especially compared with having thousands of possibilities available in the form of plug-ins. My process was generally to choose a small palette of sound sources for each track, record the main parts, and then reshape and develop them through processing. For example, every synthesizer part on “True Connection” came from the Waldorf Pulse 2. Most of the basslines on the album were created with an analogue clone of the Roland SH-101, which I also used to design many of the drum sounds, while the Acid lines came from the Behringer TD-3. Another synthesizer that played a major role throughout the album was the Model D, and I also incorporated parts I had recorded years earlier with my Roland JX-3P. On the software side, I used Ableton’s stock plug-ins alongside Massive and Omnisphere. Massive was the only synthesizer used on “Human Control,” while Omnisphere appears more sparingly on some of the other tracks, mainly providing polyphonic textures. I also enjoy running synthesizers through effects pedals to create new tones and textures, while the vocals were processed using the Roland VT-4 and a variety of VST effects. Ultimately, the main focus was to get as much character and variety as possible from a relatively small and carefully chosen set of tools. Q: With this album, you explore themes such as digital identity, technology, artificial validation, and the relationship between humans and machines. Could you tell us a little more about these themes, and to what extent did they influence your decision to release the album on vinyl? To me, the physical format almost feels like a response to – or a reaction against – the increasingly digital nature of our lives. And if so, why vinyl rather than cassette? Jesu: That was exactly the idea. Releasing the album on vinyl was, in many ways, a reaction against the digitalisation of almost every aspect of our lives. Particularly since the pandemic, it often feels as though people’s lives have been reduced to the online alter egos they create on platforms such as Instagram – showing the world only what they want others to see and projecting lifestyles that they are not necessarily living in reality. Releasing a record on vinyl had also been unfinished business for me with Espacio Cielo, so my own album felt like the perfect opportunity to take that step. There was an economic reason as well: digital sales are falling every year as listening increasingly shifts towards streaming platforms such as Spotify, yet the royalties these services pay are extremely unfair. Sometimes you barely earn enough to buy a hamburger, which makes it very difficult for an independent label to remain financially sustainable. I also feel that digital music is more ephemeral. It disappears more quickly, becomes outdated faster and struggles to hold people’s attention. A vinyl record has a physical presence and a sense of permanence: people tend to spend more time with it, and it can remain part of their lives for years. In that sense, the format became a natural extension of the album’s concept. To be honest, I never seriously considered releasing it on cassette. It is a very nostalgic format, but I also think that very few people still own the equipment needed to play tapes. Of course, the same issue exists to some extent with vinyl, but many DJs have kept their Technics turntables, and the fact that the company has released new models such as the MK7 gives me some reason for optimism. Vinyl also has a much stronger connection to my own history as a DJ and to the culture surrounding this music. From now on, we plan to slow down the label’s digital release schedule and gradually release more records on vinyl. Who knows – perhaps in a few years we will release exclusively on vinyl. It is something I am seriously considering. Q: Where do you draw the line today between human control and the control we voluntarily surrender to technology? In what sense do you see the title and concept of “Human Control” as a warning, an observation, or perhaps even a personal confession? How do you see humans evolving alongside technological progress, and what role do you think the musician will play in that relationship? Jesu: That boundary is becoming increasingly blurred. There is no denying that we will benefit enormously from technological progress and that it will make many aspects of our lives easier. However, when it comes to art and culture, I believe we need to preserve certain principles and ensure that convenience and automation do not replace human intention, creativity and genuine expression. In that sense, “Human Control” is both an observation and a warning. Technology itself is not the enemy; the real question is how much control and creative autonomy we are willing to surrender to it. We should remain the ones making the decisions, with technology serving as a tool rather than dictating the creative process. At the same time, I think a counter-movement is beginning to emerge – one that will bring back a greater appreciation for craftsmanship, physical formats and live music. I am already seeing clubs programming exclusively live sets, as well as all-vinyl nights, which I find very encouraging. Perhaps the musician’s role in this new relationship will be precisely to preserve that human element: spontaneity, imperfection and a genuine connection with the audience. Q: Do you also perform your Parissior tracks live, or do they mainly form part of your DJ sets? How does that work in practice, and what can we expect from Parissior in the near future? Jesu: I have always considered myself more of a DJ than a producer, even though, since the pandemic, I have actually spent more time producing than performing. I love playing DJ sets, and while I already have enough of my own material prepared to develop a full live show, the right opportunity has not yet presented itself. For the moment, Parissior’s music therefore appears mainly within my DJ sets. I have performed hybrid sets using hardware, but fees are sometimes so limited today that paying for additional luggage to transport equipment becomes impractical. The same applies to vinyl: I play vinyl locally, but when I travel, I usually perform with CDJs for exactly the same reason. Because of my day job, I only play around five or six gigs a year, and promoters generally approach me to perform DJ sets. However, I would definitely like to explore the live format when the right opportunity and conditions come along. About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He began DJing professionally in his native Cantabria in 2001 under his own name, playing Techno and House. In 2004 he moved to Salamanca, where he became a resident DJ at venues including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz, and later opened his own venue, Clavel Ocho, whose upstairs floor, Espacio Cielo, was dedicated to electronic music. He started producing around 2004 and has released more than 600 tracks under various aliases. He created the Parissior alias in 2011 to explore Electro, Italo-Disco and EBM-influenced sounds beyond his earlier productions. Parissior has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly through Espacio Cielo, the label he revived from his former venue’s name, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control”, Parissior’s first full-length album, was released on Espacio Cielo in collaboration with Mots Music. Side-Line reviewed the album in September 2026, describing it as a mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. This interview follows that review.

items.body: Hermidgets, the anonymous Italian dark synthpop project, has released “Like Moths” alongside an official video. The single is out now through Bandcamp and is the fourth preview of Hermidgets’ third album, expected in early 2027. “Like Moths” was mixed by Matteo Sandri and mastered by Giovanni Versari. A bass-heavy opening gives way to rhythmic, buzzing synthesizers, with Hermidgets’ baritone vocal set against a danceable groove and a bright, wiry synth line that recurs through the track. The lyrics follow two people drawn into a relationship whose destructive pull has become part of its appeal, turning surrender into something close to devotional: “Learn how to pray for the pleasure of having nothing.” The video, directed around a concept developed independently of the song, was inspired by French artist Olivier de Sagazan. Shot in black and white, it isolates Hermidgets’ head and shoulders as white modeling clay obscures and distorts his features throughout the performance, with black pigment introduced later in the video. The project keeps its members unidentified, and the clay imagery extends that approach by withholding a clear view of the performer’s face. Like Moths by Hermidgets About Hermidgets Hermidgets is an Italian electronic project that does not identify its members, combining distorted synthpop and darkwave songwriting with self-produced visuals. The debut album, “The Mire,” was released in November 2020 and included the songs “This Is Over” and “Nothing’s Perfect.” The singles “A Flaw” and “Perks” followed in 2021, and “Meaninglessness” and “We Tend to Disappear” appeared on the mini-album “NIHIL” in June 2024, recorded with a limited setup of two analog synthesizers, drum samples and voice. Hermidgets began previewing a third album with the single “Fall Apart” in July 2025, followed by “Sundown” in December 2025 and “Could I Be Better” in March 2026, a song that revisits “Could Be Better” from the 2020 debut. “Like Moths,” released in September 2026, is the fourth single from that album cycle, with the full album expected in early 2027.

Get Up by Mass Minor “This song is a conversation with God at 169 BPM about sin, money, mortality and the things we sacrifice our lives to,” Martin says of the track. “It comes from this idea of asking God to save us from problems we created ourselves. Maybe it’s not God’s job to save us. Maybe we need to fix our own shit. You’re the one holding the light. Get up.” A music video for “Get Up”, directed by Teresa Jolie and edited by Beau Loy, accompanies the release. “Get Up” follows “Nowhere Now”, issued as a single in late July. Both songs are set to appear on a new Mass Minor album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due out in late February 2027 on Metropolis Records. About Mass Minor Mass Minor is the Austin, Texas-based project of Andrew J. Martin Jr., who blends atmospheric synths and driving guitars with post-punk, synth-pop and alternative rock influences. Martin self-released the project’s debut album, “Become Each Other”, in 2020, followed by a run of singles later collected on EPs. The project built a presence in the dark alternative scene through radio support, multiple SXSW appearances and shows alongside acts including Twin Tribes, Ultra Sunn, TRAITRS, Vision Video, Urban Heat and Sacred Skin. Mass Minor signed to Metropolis Records and released the single “Nowhere Now” in July 2026, followed by “Get Up” on 2 October 2026. Both tracks lead into the project’s next album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due in late February 2027.

items.body: Susanne Jonsson and Jan Strandqvist of the Swedish band Red Mecca have returned after a hiatus. Their time away, however, was marked by intense and deeply painful experiences: Susanne’s sister was murdered and her relationship fell apart, while Jan struggled with addiction. Sometimes, nothing seems better than returning to creative expression—in their case, by making a new album. This record clearly holds great significance for them, even though the music remains true to Red Mecca’s signature sound and style. It is a polished album, balancing understated, sensitive, and refined tracks with a somewhat ‘harder’ Synth-Pop style. The songs are expertly crafted and beautifully sung by Susanne Jonsson, a vocalist who has nothing left to prove. Personally, I prefer their Electro-Pop style—which occasionally hints at EBM elements—as it really showcases their talent for creating great music. While some tracks may lack a definitive climax, I believe the choice to create a more restrained work was deliberate. This may not be my favorite album by the duo, but it stands as a significant and healing production in their career. (Rating:7½). Listen to “I’m On The Outside”: I’m On The Outside by Red Mecca About Red Mecca Red Mecca was set up by Jan Strandqvist, originally with vocalist Frida Madeleine, who left after four albums and was replaced by Susanne Jonsson. The Swedish duo released “Truth” in 2019, followed by the albums “Away” (2021) and “Stay” (2023), all on Massproduktion. Strandqvist discussed the band’s history, including a 2016 Swedish Manifest Award win and a soundtrack placement on “Killing Eve”, in a 2021 Side-Line Click Interview.

items.body: On Orthodox Tapes, London-based artist Andrew Sherwell dives into the dusty vortex of the past, using the style of hauntology to pursue a place of personal recollection and warm remembrance. Hauntology doesn’t usually highlight warmth. The Caretaker uses it to examine the horrifying decline of the mind while Pye Corner Audio uses it as a kind of ghost-box through which spirits and cool, VHS-recorded synths enter; it’s a style reeking of decay. Orthodox Tapes runs close to the latter because it broadcasts not only the music of the past but a life of the past. In this instance, nocturnal tape loops and creased-up field recordings summon up the many experiences of Andrew’s grandfather, who once travelled back and forth through the Balkans, Central Europe and Southern Russia during the inter-war period. Andrew would spend school holidays at his grandfather’s house, where, as an old man, he would recount his many adventures over a bedtime story. The evening light fused with deep recollections and fantastical tales of bygone days: encounters with local people and their folk tales, stories of Orthodox bishops and beautiful princesses, of demons lurking in pure daylight and angels in human form, of days spent in endless forests and nights camped out on the grasslands, staring up at the bright silver moon and the sequined stars. Needless to say, these stories had a powerful impact on Andrew as a child, and the music is equally mysterious, sprinkled in memory-dust, bewitching the listener with its world of ambient sighs, dim crackles and dusty echoes. The projector starts up, whirring away in the background as a ghostly chorus appears, slowly drawing the listener deeper and deeper into its past life. Church bells clank in an old town, and vapours rise out of the slumbering world. Orthodox Tapes slinks away from reality, descending into the deep pools of sleep. Mermaids are masqueraded in a curdled pool of unclear water and fantastical things swim underneath. This isn’t the real world – it’s something better. It’s a place of tranquil escape. These voices lie on the pillow-soft clouds of a beautiful (if strange) dream. Because of his personal connection, love seeps out of the music, giving the airy atmosphere a romanticized vibe: it’s the scent of old times and of unbreakable ties, of comfort and deep familiarity…and of ultimate rest. But this was a tumultuous time – some believed it to be the end of days – and the drones slip into foggy voids, too. ‘Beware Koschei’s Visit’ is one example of the mood’s relegation, and that’s how the record ends, expressing both sides of the story: the narrator and the listener, the artist and the audience…the magic of childhood, oblivious to a frightening world on the other side of that bedroom door and the untold horrors across the sea. www.whitelabrecs.bandcamp.com

items.body: Matt Carlson is one half of Portland, Oregon duo Golden Retriever, and has also released a number of solo recordings under his own name. His latest, for French label Shelter Press, demonstrates his interest in linguistics and language games, combining heavily processed and manipulated voices with blooping and chirping modular synthesis. Sometimes the voices are squeezed to the point of wordlessness, simply pitched tones that are never quite simply pitched tones because of their still-recognisable source in human speech. At other times, such as in the tracks “The Game” and “An Enhanced Interrogation of Authenticity”, the meanings of words and their modes of presentation are played with to dizzying and disorienting effect. In some ways, “The View From Nowhere” reminds me of the work of US artist Bruce Nauman, particularly his classic video works such as “Good Boy Bad Boy” and “Clown Torture”. In these works, Nauman uses repetition, recontextualisation, and similar techniques to transform language into sculpture-like objects, revealing its inherent absurdity and arbitrariness. The same devices are frequently used by Carlson, but while Nauman was primarily concerned with critiquing the use of language to exercise power and inflict violence, the Portlander seems genuinely interested in the intricacies of linguistic science and the ways in which, through repetition and social injunction, the meanings of language gestures come to be attributed or undermined. The synthesised elements of the album reflect this theme, with rapid-fire pulses, sweeping filters and pans, and shimmering textures mirroring the complex and constantly shifting sands of verbal discourse. The vocal sounds mingle freely with the instrumental ones, being multiplied, echoed, and filtered to the point where they often become rhythmic and tonal elements in themselves. While genuine in its attempts to engage in a musical way with linguistic theory, “The View From Nowhere” retains Nauman’s penchant for the absurd and for off-kilter humour, turning what could have been quite a dry, impenetrable exercise into something intriguing and fun.   The View From Nowhere by Matt Carlson   Matt Carlson Shelter Press

items.body: Lines The Polish clarinetist and composer Waclaw Zimpel has played in numerous bands over the years, including, most recently, his own Waclaw Zimpel Quartet, and the Waclaw Zimpel To Tu Orchestra, with which he released the notable albums Stone Fog (2013) and Nature Moves (2014) respectively, on the excellent jazz label For Tune. Lines is his first solo effort. “What I had in mind was mostly polyphonic music but I couldn’t see a point in working on this with other players,” says Zimpel. “First of all, I wanted to perform most of the melodic lines on clarinets. I had a very precise vision of how those lines should be composed and it felt very natural to perform all of them by myself. Secondly, this album is mostly written not improvised so I had no problem recording track after track feeling that some of live-performance spontaneity is being lost,” he adds. Zimpel is something of a scholar. Over the years he’s delved into the musical traditions of India, Japan, and Morocco and researched the roots of improvisation from liturgical music to African trance. With Lines, the Polish clarinetist constructs an intricate sonic framework of parallel chords that attain a ritualistic effect by virtue of their varying configuration. He explores the depths of sound by unhinging any linearity in time that might carry a narrative intention in order to unveil new projections of aural space. Different musical environments are suggested, although the opening track, Alupa – Pappa, locates the album firmly in the Minimalist camp and sets the tone. “I think that you can sense this characteristic approach to space and sound is audible on all compositions, despite the fact that they differ between themselves. What might be the main common denominator is the inspiration I drew from the pioneers of American minimalism, like La Monte Young and Terry Riley. Some parts of ‘Lines’ are in a way a paraphrasis of their formal ideas from the 60’s and 70’s. I also believe that ‘Deo Gratias’, being a Renaissance canon in its own way, also fits this concept as a prophecy of minimalism composed 500 years earlier,” explains Waclaw. Notwithstanding the subtly shifting patterns of the album, it would be misleading to think, that Lines is just a modern take on Minimalism, even if the debt to Reich, Riley & co is undeniable, as the title track testifies. Moreover, the philological approach is guaranteed by the use of Hammond organ and fender Rhodes, which appear elsewhere in the album. Zimpel’s take, though, is wider in scope. As he mentions, with Deo Gratias he also looks back at the work of the Flemish 15th century singer, choirmaster, and composer Johannes Ockeghem. Zimpel mimics the density of events in Ockeghem’s polyphonic music, often giving each new voice he introduces throughout the album, something different to say about any melodic or rhythmic idea proposed by another. This is achieved in a remarkably unlabored and seemingly effortless manner. The emphasis is always on the emotional undercurrent that seeps through loops and tones. The organic quality of the sound is mesmerizing in its flow. The rhythmic spell is only eventually broken midway through the closing track Tak Picture, only to resurface briefly before finally grinding to a halt. Lines by Wac?aw Zimpel Lines is out on Instant Classics on February 5, 2016 A beautiful black and white video of Waclaw Zimpel performing lines can be seen here www.waclawzimpel.pl
